t: Count Commas in Range — Digit-Length Layers
o: A number with d digits carries floor((d-1)/3) commas. Example 1: 1000..1002 are 4-digit numbers with 1 comma each → 3. Example 2: everything below 1000 has ≤ 3 digits → 0. Rather than formatting every number, count how many numbers in [1, n] have each digit-length d and multiply by (d-1)//3.
k: Full layers contribute 9·10^(d-1) numbers each; the top layer contributes n - 10^(d-1) + 1.
With n ≤ 1e5 only lengths 1..6 appear, so at most 1 comma per number.

a.i: For each integer, count its digits and add (digits-1)//3. Perfectly fine for n ≤ 1e5.
a.t: O(n log n) — digit counting per number

a.i: Group [1, n] by digit length. Every complete layer [10^(d-1), 10^d - 1] has 9·10^(d-1) numbers with (d-1)//3 commas; the partial top layer has n - 10^(d-1) + 1 numbers.
s: Let d = number of digits of n.
For each full length L < d, add 9·10^(L-1) · ((L-1)//3).
a.t: O(log n) — one pass over digit lengths

w: Either works at these constraints; the layer method scales to astronomically large n and is the one to present. Pitfalls: the loop starts at L = 4 (numbers below 1000 have no commas), and the top-layer count is inclusive of both endpoints. Follow-up: count commas up to 10^18 (same formula, 64-bit arithmetic).
